title: Former OPP witnessed police struggle
article: Wearing casual summer clothes, former OPP Insp. Jim McDonnell was going for a simple bike ride to the bank machine on a July morning three years ago.
Little did he know he would become a witness to a Barrie police confrontation that left 48-year-old Dennis Melton dead.
Melton was yelling and screaming while walking along Bayfield Street near the Kozlov Centre when Constables Dave Edgar and Clayton Speers approached him.
He slashed Speers' throat and was then tackled by Edgar. Edgar's throat was also cut, then Melton was shot and killed. The officers recovered.
The Special Investigations Unit has cleared Edgar and Speers in Melton's death, but since he died during a police interaction, an inquest was called.
McDonnell took the stand Monday as the Coroner's Inquest began.

Coroner Maarthen Reinders explained to the jury a Coroner's Inquest doesn't find legal responsibility for the outcome, and they must decide if the cause of death was natural, accidental, suicidal, homicidal or undetermined.
McDonnell joined the scene on his bicycle that morning after having just retired from the OPP just five days earlier.

"I noticed a patrol car pass me, it (turned on the flashing four-way lights and) pulled over to the right curb and stopped," said McDonnell, who is trained in hostage scenarios and was a commander during the Caledonia standoff in 2006.
He soon saw it wasn't a radar stop.
"I approached the rear of the cruiser and saw the second officer with a heavy set individual. The other officer stopped on the sidewalk, about three metres (away)."
He described Melton as having "disheveled hair with a beard" and he was dressed in an overcoat.
"(Melton) had a knapsack and was clutching it with his left hand towards his chest. He was making a gesture with his right hand with a fist movement back and forth."
He saw Melton was agitated and said he was concerned for the safety of the officers.
One of the concerns McDonnell had was the proximity of Const. Clayton Speers to Melton.
McDonnell said he normally trains officers to stay within an arm's length of a subject.

"I looked at the situation and felt something was amiss. Melton looked me directly in the eye. I looked at him and he looked at me. Between (his) actions and his voice raised, I was alarmed based on my previous experience."
Not wanting to distract the officers on the job, McDonnell rode his bike around to the Kozlov Centre parking lot near Bayfield and Heather streets.
"I was concerned about the situation unfolding, but at the same point in time I didn't want to intervene/distract the officers," said McDonnell.
He also didn't have any ID to let them know who he was.
"I believe they handled it in a textbook manner," he told the jury.

"In my view, they had the grounds to take him into custody. (Melton) had borderline assaultive behaviour and under the Mental Health Act felt the officers could have taken him into custody for his own safety."
Not noticing any weapon, McDonnell decided to continue his trip to the bank machine and it wasn't until he was back outside minutes later that he heard gunshots.
"I didn't immediately associate the situation I had left with the gunshots. Then I saw a cruiser coming down Cundles Road with its lights and siren on."
McDonnell rode back to the scene and saw Melton on the ground.

"I remained there to assist in any way I could. Another civilian approached me and said there were keys on the ground. They could be a key part of evidence, so I got the attention of a uniformed officer and I made sure no one touched those keys."
McDonnell said he later went to the Barrie police station to give his statement.
Other witnesses are expected on the stand throughout the next few weeks as the inquest continues.
